goldens.comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Incomplete double-checked locking: missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock in webassets.go:41-50, causing duplicate asset tree re-walk/re-parse and cache overwrite instead of early return
New concurrency/synchronization logic in webassets.go has zero test coverage, meaning regressions like deadlocks or data races would surface only in production

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an RWMutex around a global cache in GetWebAssets, but it does not show anything about the test suite. From this snippet alone you can’t verify that there is “zero test coverage” for this new synchronization logic; existing tests elsewhere could still exercise it. The claim about regressions only surfacing in production is also speculative and not diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Dev-mode path (cfg.Env == setting.Dev) takes a write lock on every request even though it never uses the cache, serializing web-assets endpoint requests in Dev

adjudication.rationale: In `GetWebAssets`, after the dev-mode cache-bypass check (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil { return ret, nil }`), the code unconditionally takes `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and defers `Unlock()`. That means when `cfg.Env == setting.Dev` the function will still take the write lock for the whole remainder of the call, which can serialize concurrent requests to this endpoint even though dev mode intentionally doesn’t return the cached `entryPointAssetsCache` in the early-return path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Double-checked-locking fast path is incomplete: after acquiring the write lock the function never re-checks the cache, so concurrent cold-start requests all recompute the full asset scan

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a read-lock fast path and then a write lock before computing, but it does not include the remainder of `GetWebAssets`. From the provided hunk we cannot verify that the function "never re-checks" the cache after acquiring the write lock; that could occur later outside the shown lines. Therefore the finding cannot be confirmed from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cached *dtos.EntryPointAssets pointer is shared with all callers concurrently with no copy or immutability contract, so any downstream mutation causes a data race the mutex doesn't protect against

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a global cached pointer `entryPointAssetsCache` guarded by an RWMutex and returns the cached pointer directly (`return ret, nil`). The mutex only protects reads/writes of the pointer itself, not concurrent mutations of the referenced `dtos.EntryPointAssets` after it’s returned. If any caller mutates the returned struct, that would bypass the mutex and could race with other callers. The diff doesn’t show any such mutation, so it’s a real design/contract concern but not a verifiable defect from this snippet alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Dev mode serializes every request because the ret != nil fast path is skipped and every goroutine unconditionally acquires the exclusive entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() for the full filesystem scan, turning parallel asset scans into sequential ones

adjudication.rationale: In GetWebAssets, after the RLock/RUnlock fast-path, the code unconditionally acquires entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() (with defer Unlock) regardless of cfg.Env. Since the early return is gated by `cfg.Env != setting.Dev`, dev mode will always skip the cache return and thus always take the exclusive lock, serializing concurrent callers through the rest of the function (likely including the filesystem scan). This is a real diff-grounded performance/concurrency concern rather than a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Missing re-check (or skip-locking when cfg.Env == setting.Dev) so dev mode never touches the cache, matching pre-existing semantics

adjudication.rationale: In the new code, `GetWebAssets` always RLocks/reads `entryPointAssetsCache` and then always takes the write `Lock()` (via `defer Unlock()`) even when `cfg.Env == setting.Dev`. Previously, dev mode didn’t consult the cache at all and didn’t serialize calls on a global mutex. Also, after releasing the RLock and before acquiring the Lock, another goroutine could populate the cache; without a re-check under the write lock, this can lead to redundant recomputation (though not necessarily incorrect).

adjudication_records.issue_text: PR scope drift: title is 'Frontend Asset Optimization' but visible diff is only a concurrency-correctness change to a global cache

adjudication.rationale: The finding depends on the PR title ('Frontend Asset Optimization') and claims scope drift versus the diff, but the title/PR metadata is not part of the provided diff. From the diff alone, we can only see a concurrency-related change (adding an RWMutex around a global cache), not whether it conflicts with the PR’s stated scope.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Missing nil re-check of ret after acquiring the write lock, resulting in incomplete double-checked locking

adjudication.rationale: The diff implements an RLock fast-path (return cached `ret` when non-dev and non-nil), then unconditionally takes the write lock and proceeds to recompute without re-checking whether `entryPointAssetsCache` was populated by another goroutine while waiting. That makes the double-checked locking pattern incomplete and can cause redundant work under concurrent calls, but it doesn’t clearly break correctness from what’s shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Under concurrent cold-start load, losing goroutines serially rebuild assets while holding the exclusive lock, causing duplicate work and lock contention

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an RWMutex and does an initial RLock read into `ret`, but if `ret` is nil it unconditionally takes the exclusive `Lock()` and proceeds without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache` under the write lock. With concurrent cold-start requests, multiple goroutines can observe nil before any cache fill, then queue on the write lock and each will rebuild sequentially while holding the lock, causing duplicate work and contention. This is a concrete, diff-grounded concurrency/performance issue rather than a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Serialized rebuilds block readers that could get cache hits, causing thundering-herd filesystem walks and request latency spikes after process restart

adjudication.rationale: In GetWebAssets, the code reads the cache under RLock, unlocks, and only then takes the write Lock to rebuild. There is no second cache check after acquiring the write lock. If multiple goroutines see ret == nil concurrently (e.g., right after restart), they will serialize on entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() and each will rebuild even if a previous goroutine already populated entryPointAssetsCache, causing avoidable filesystem walks and blocking readers that could have returned a cache hit.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Lock is not double-checked: after acquiring entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock(), the code never re-reads entryPointAssetsCache under the write lock before rebuilding, allowing concurrent first requests to each serially rebuild the full asset set instead of one rebuild followed by cache hits

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an RLock/RUnlock fast-path, then unconditionally takes entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() without re-checking entryPointAssetsCache under the write lock. That means two concurrent callers can both miss the cache, and even if the first fills entryPointAssetsCache before the second acquires the write lock, the second will still rebuild instead of returning the cached value. This is a real, diff-grounded inefficiency (lack of double-checked locking), but it doesn’t demonstrate incorrect behavior from the shown code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Double-checked locking pattern in the asset cache is not truly double-checked since the second read is not re-verified under the write lock, risking writer starvation

adjudication.rationale: The diff implements a read-then-write locking scheme: it reads `entryPointAssetsCache` under `RLock`, and if nil it releases and then unconditionally takes `Lock()` without re-checking the cache. That means it is not a true double-checked lock and can lead to redundant recomputation if another goroutine populates the cache between the `RUnlock()` and `Lock()`. However, the claimed "writer starvation" is not evidenced by the diff (and Go’s `RWMutex` generally blocks new readers once a writer is pending), so the concrete issue here is inefficiency/extra work rather than a verifiable correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Write lock in pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:45-49 is held across the entire asset-loading section with no double-check after acquisition, serializing all concurrent asset requests behind one disk-read

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` is acquired immediately after the initial cache read/fast-path check, and there is no second check of `entryPointAssetsCache` after the write lock is obtained. This means concurrent callers that all observe `nil` will queue on the write lock and, once they each acquire it, will proceed into the (presumably expensive) asset-loading path even if a prior goroutine has already populated the cache. That’s a performance/concurrency issue (unnecessary serialization and repeated disk work), not a correctness defect visible in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: In Dev mode where cfg.Env == setting.Dev bypasses the read cache, every request takes the write lock causing redundant re-load on a thundering herd

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an RWMutex and does take the write lock on the slow path (including when cfg.Env == setting.Dev), but that does not create a “thundering herd”: the write lock serializes callers rather than allowing concurrent redundant reloads. Also, bypassing the cache in Dev mode is intentional per the existing condition (cfg.Env != setting.Dev) and is not shown as a newly introduced defect here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Dev-env requests serialize on the write lock because the read-fast-path is skipped when cfg.Env == setting.Dev, causing head-of-line blocking on concurrent asset requests during development

adjudication.rationale: In `GetWebAssets`, the function always takes the write lock (`entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`) after the initial read section, and only returns early on the read-fast-path when `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil`. For `cfg.Env == setting.Dev`, that fast-path is intentionally skipped, so every concurrent dev request will contend on the single write lock and serialize through the rest of the function under that lock (due to `defer Unlock()`), which can cause head-of-line blocking. This is a performance/concurrency concern rather than a correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Write-lock section may not re-check entryPointAssetsCache != nil before rebuilding, causing redundant rebuild and overwrite on concurrent Prod cold-cache requests

adjudication.rationale: After the initial RLock/RUnlock, the code unconditionally takes a write lock and proceeds without re-checking whether `entryPointAssetsCache` was populated by another goroutine in the meantime (`entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock(); defer ...`). This can cause redundant rebuild work (and likely overwrite) on concurrent non-dev cold-cache requests. The diff does not show any correctness break, just avoidable extra work due to missing double-check under the write lock.
